extracted.intended_audience: academics, university PR staff, and science journalists interested in science communication and press-release practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative points about producing and assessing academic press releases so they do not exaggerate or mislead the public; covers transparency, authorship, how evidence is presented, and the responsibilities of journalists and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggeration / not misleading the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic press releases routinely exaggerate scientific findings and mislead the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post cites empirical research showing routine exaggeration, and gives the BMJ's own misleading press release as an example ('hopelessly and entirely misleading'). Press releases should not overstate results, imply causation from association, or sensationalise findings. They should use cautious language that matches the evidence (avoid definitive claims when evidence is tentative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and shame (make outputs transparent and accountable)
rubrics_metrics.description: These ideas revolve largely around transparency and shame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations emphasise disclosure (who produced the release, conflicts, data availability) and public accountability so that misleading statements can be challenged. Transparency measures could include clear attribution, links to the full paper and data, and visible records of who authorised the release to create reputational incentives against exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship / stated responsibility for press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should have authorship stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments recommend making PR authors and responsible scientists publicly identified so individuals and organisations take responsibility ('make the PR companies take public responsibility for what they say'). One suggestion: 'all press releases must be attached PIs and co-Is next grant proposal.' Include contact names and accountable sign-offs on releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists should critically appraise evidence rather than copying releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers don't expect journalists to be secretaries. Readers expect journalists to add value by critically appraising the evidence for claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should not act as press-release stenographers. They should assess study design, limitations, magnitude of effect, conflicts of interest, and present context rather than repeating spin. News coverage should add independent evaluation, not merely amplify PR claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present absolute risks/benefits, not only relative effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reporting relative rather than absolute benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases (and ensuing coverage) should give absolute risk/benefit numbers or NNT where relevant, not only relative percentages that can mislead about clinical importance. Include baseline rates and clear numerical context to avoid exaggerating apparent effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective or post hoc reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not promote 'using post hoc data ± selectively' or emphasise unplanned subgroup findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases should clearly state whether results/analyses were pre-specified, and should not highlight post hoc or exploratory analyses as if they were confirmatory. Disclose which outcomes were primary vs secondary and avoid cherry-picking favourable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for biased sampling, publication bias and selective publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of 'biased sampling & publishing' that can distort reported findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releases should situate findings within the broader evidence base, acknowledge relevant negative studies or limitations in sampling, and not give an impression that a single positive result overturns existing evidence without qualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise institutional incentives that encourage exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: The focus on 'Impact' creates incentives to exaggerate the impact of research when applying for grants and when publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any rubric for press releases must consider perverse incentives (career/reward structures) that push academics and communications teams towards hype. Remedies should address institutional drivers and not solely blame individual scientists; policy changes may be needed to align incentives with accurate communication.
